Infrastructure as code for modern cloud and on-premises environments. This book starts from what a configuration means and ends at a production change pipeline.

The OpenTofu Story: From Terraform to Open Source
OpenTofu is the open-source continuation of the Terraform language and workflow, under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. This chapter is the history you need before you trust a module written for the other binary.

title: The OpenTofu Story: From Terraform to Open Source
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Say what OpenTofu is, and what it deliberately kept from Terraform
Place the August 2023 license change on a timeline
Tell a 1.5-era configuration from a feature that exists on only one of the two tools
Choose OpenTofu for a reason you can write down

title: The OpenTofu Story: From Terraform to Open Source
section: What Is OpenTofu?
text:
What Is OpenTofu?
OpenTofu is a command-line tool, tofu, that reads HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) and reconciles it with infrastructure through provider plugins. You declare resources. It builds a plan. You apply the plan. It records what it created in a state file.
The project is a fork of Terraform as it stood under MPL 2.0. The Linux Foundation hosts it. In April 2025 the project was accepted into the CNCF sandbox. Providers are not rewritten by OpenTofu. The same provider plugins Terraform uses are published for the OpenTofu registry at registry.opentofu.org, and the protocol between tofu and those plugins is the Terraform plugin protocol.
This book pins 1.13.2, released 21 October 2026. The 1.13 series is the supported line until 1 August 2027. Terraform’s version numbers are not OpenTofu’s. In the same month Terraform’s current release was in the 1.17 series. Equal numbers do not mean equal features, and a higher Terraform number does not mean OpenTofu is behind on every axis. State encryption shipped in OpenTofu 1.7 and is not a Terraform language feature.

title: The OpenTofu Story: From Terraform to Open Source
section: The Terraform License Change: A Turning Point
text:
The Terraform License Change: A Turning Point
Through Terraform 1.5.x, HashiCorp shipped Terraform under MPL 2.0. On 10 August 2023 HashiCorp moved future releases of Terraform, and of several other products, to the Business Source License (BSL, also written BUSL) 1.1. The BSL is source-available. It is not an Open Source Initiative license. It restricts using the licensed software to offer a competing product.
1.5.x remained the last MPL release. Configurations, state, and the provider protocol up to that line are the common ancestor. Everything HashiCorp shipped as Terraform 1.6 and later is under the BSL. Everything OpenTofu shipped is under MPL 2.0, starting from that ancestor and then diverging on purpose.
The practical effect for an engineer: you can read either codebase, and your lawyer will care which binary you ship inside a product. The practical effect for a module: a file that only uses language from 1.5 loads in both. A file that uses a feature added on one side after the fork needs the binary that has it.

title: The OpenTofu Story: From Terraform to Open Source
section: HashiCorp vs. Linux Foundation: The Fork That Changed Everything
text:
HashiCorp vs. Linux Foundation: The Fork That Changed Everything
The fork was announced as an open-source Terraform, then named OpenTofu, and contributed to the Linux Foundation so the trademark and the governance were not a single vendor’s. The first stable OpenTofu release was 1.6 in January 2024, compatible with the 1.5 language and ready to keep moving.
Governance is the part that is easy to skip and expensive to misunderstand. HashiCorp (later under IBM) decides Terraform’s product direction, including HCP Terraform, Stacks, and Sentinel. The OpenTofu technical steering committee decides OpenTofu’s direction in public issues and RFCs. A feature that is a commercial control plane on one side may be a CLI feature, or absent, on the other.
The registry split follows the same line. registry.terraform.io is HashiCorp’s. registry.opentofu.org is the community registry. Provider namespaces such as hashicorp/aws exist on both because the providers themselves stayed available. When you write source = "hashicorp/aws" in this book, tofu init resolves it through the OpenTofu registry unless you override the host.

title: The OpenTofu Story: From Terraform to Open Source
section: OpenTofu vs. Terraform: Compatibility, Differences, and Trade-offs
text:
OpenTofu vs. Terraform: Compatibility, Differences, and Trade-offs
Treat compatibility as three layers.








Layer
What still matches
What has diverged




Language shared with 1.5
Resources, modules, count, for_each, import blocks, checks, the testing framework’s early form
—


State
State written by Terraform through 1.5.x is the documented drop-in. Later state can often be migrated, and you test that migration. You do not assume it
Client-side encryption of state and plan files is OpenTofu (1.7+)


Later language
Both grew ephemeral resources, write-only attributes, and provider for_each on their own timelines
OpenTofu 1.13 adds convert and assumenotnull to tame unknown values at plan time. Terraform 1.13+ added Stacks, a query workflow, and a commercial policy product. Version numbers crossed and the features did not



Other OpenTofu marks you will meet in later chapters: the .tofu file extension (1.8) for files that must not be read by Terraform, variables and locals inside module sources and backends (1.8), OCI registry addresses (1.10), S3 locking without a separate lock table (1.10), and the enabled meta-argument (1.11).
1.13 also removes WinRM from the file and remote-exec provisioners, changes base64gzip output bytes, requires macOS 13 or newer, and drops official 32-bit builds. Windows on ARM64 is a supported package. Read the series changelog before you bump a production pin. Chapter 14 is that upgrade habit.

title: The OpenTofu Story: From Terraform to Open Source
section: When to Choose OpenTofu (and When Not To)
text:
When to Choose OpenTofu (and When Not To)
Choose OpenTofu when the license has to be MPL, when you want client-side state encryption in the CLI, or when you want the roadmap set by a foundation project rather than a commercial control plane. Choose it when your modules stay within the shared language, or within OpenTofu features you have pinned.
Stay on Terraform when a system you already pay for requires the Terraform binary: an HCP Terraform workspace, a Sentinel policy pack you are not ready to rewrite as Open Policy Agent, or a module that uses a Terraform-only feature you have confirmed OpenTofu rejects. “We might use Stacks later” is not a reason. A failing tofu init on a required feature is.
Do not run both binaries against the same state. Pick one per state file, pin it in .terraform-version or your runtime manager, and review the plan under that pin.

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
text:
Architecture and Core Concepts
Six words carry the rest of the book: configuration, plan, state, provider, resource, data source. This chapter defines them before any cloud account appears.

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Separate what you write from what tofu does
Walk init, plan, apply, and destroy without memorising flags
Explain why state exists
Tell a resource from a data source

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: The Declarative Paradigm: What You Define vs. What Happens
text:
The Declarative Paradigm: What You Define vs. What Happens
You write the desired end state. You do not write the API calls. A resource block says “this object should exist with these arguments.” OpenTofu’s job is to notice the difference between that text and the recorded reality, and to call the provider until the difference is gone or the plan says it cannot be done without a destructive change.
That is declarative in the useful sense, not in the absolute sense. The order of blocks in a file is not the order of API calls. A local-exec provisioner is an imperative escape hatch, which is why chapter 10 discourages it. Arguments you set are desired state. Attributes the provider fills in (an id, a generated name) are observed state. Mixing those up is the first source of plans that fight you.
Idempotence is the promise: apply, then apply again, and the second plan is empty when nothing outside the configuration changed. Drift is the world editing itself. A person in a console, or another tool, changes an object the state still tracks. The next plan proposes to put it back. That proposal is the point of the tool.

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: OpenTofu’s Execution Model: Plan, Apply, Destroy
text:
OpenTofu’s Execution Model: Plan, Apply, Destroy
The commands you will actually live in:









Command
Reads
Writes
Talks to the infrastructure




tofu init
required_providers, backend, modules
.terraform/, lock file
Downloads providers and modules


tofu plan
Configuration, state, data sources
A plan file if you ask
Refreshes and computes a diff


tofu apply
A plan, or it makes one and waits
State
Creates, updates, and destroys objects


tofu destroy
Configuration and state
State
Destroys what state tracks



plan is a dry run with teeth. It refreshes state by default, so it does contact APIs. It does not change infrastructure. apply with no plan file plans and then prompts. In automation you save the plan (tofu plan -out=tfplan) and apply that exact file (tofu apply tfplan) so the change a human approved is the change that runs.
Destroy is not the opposite of a git revert. It deletes the objects in state. A revert of the configuration, followed by apply, also deletes objects that disappeared from the configuration. Both are destructive. Chapter 9’s prevent_destroy is how you make a specific resource refuse.

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: Providers: The Bridge Between Configuration and Reality
text:
Providers: The Bridge Between Configuration and Reality
OpenTofu does not know what an S3 bucket is. A provider plugin does. tofu starts the plugin, hands it the resource configuration, and stores whatever identity the plugin returns.
The required_providers block names the source and the version. Init downloads the plugin and writes .terraform.lock.hcl. That lock file is how the next machine gets the same plugin build. Commit it. Chapter 6 is authentication, aliases, and version constraints. For now, the bridge is: configuration in, API calls out, attributes back.
A provider configuration block (provider "aws" { ... }) is not a resource. It is credentials, region, and endpoints for every resource of that type. No block is required for providers that need no credentials. random is the one this book applies for real.

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: Resources: The Fundamental Building Blocks
text:
Resources: The Fundamental Building Blocks
A resource has a type and a local name: resource "random_pet" "service". The address you use everywhere else is random_pet.service. The type is the provider’s. The local name is yours, unique among that type in the module.
Arguments are what you set. After apply, the state holds those plus computed attributes. The next plan compares both. Changing an argument that the provider cannot update in place produces a destroy and a create. The plan says so with -/+ or a replacement. Read that line before you approve it.
count and for_each make many instances from one block. Instances have addresses like random_pet.service["api"]. Those addresses are how state finds the object. Renaming the key is a destroy and a create unless you move the state. Chapter 9 covers moved blocks and dependencies.

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: State: Why It Exists and How It Works
text:
State: Why It Exists and How It Works
The configuration says what you want. It does not remember the id of the object it created last Tuesday. State does. State is a JSON document mapping each resource address to a provider-specific id and the attribute values from the last refresh.
Without state, the next apply would try to create a second copy, or would have to guess which remote object belongs to which block. Guessing is how tools delete the wrong thing. State is the memory that makes the guess unnecessary.
Local state is a file named terraform.tfstate in the working directory. It is enough for the pet example. It is the wrong place for anything a second person, or a pipeline, must update. Two applies against two copies of state create two worlds. Chapter 7 moves state to a backend with locking. State also stores attribute values, including ones marked sensitive. Sensitive means “do not print it in the plan UI.” It does not mean “omit it from the state file.”

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: Data Sources: Reading the World Without Creating It
text:
Data Sources: Reading the World Without Creating It
A data source reads. It does not create, update, or destroy. data "aws_ami" "latest" asks the provider a question and stores the answer for the rest of the configuration to interpolate.
Data sources are refreshed during plan. A data source that changes under you changes the plan, which is what you want when you are looking up a current AMI, and what you do not want when the lookup is a moving target you should have pinned. Prefer a resource for anything you created and now need to remember. Prefer a data source for something that already existed and is owned elsewhere.
Data sources land in state too, as a cache of the last read. They are not a second source of truth. The next refresh overwrites them.

title: Architecture and Core Concepts
section: Summary
text:
Summary

You declare the end state. OpenTofu computes the API calls
Init fetches plugins. Plan diffs. Apply changes. Destroy deletes what state tracks
Providers speak APIs. Resources are the objects. State remembers their ids
A data source reads. It does not own the object
A second apply is empty only when the world still matches the configuration and the state

Installation and Project Structure
Pin the binary before you pin the providers. This chapter installs OpenTofu 1.13.2, checks that the binary is that release, and lays out a repository that a second engineer can clone.

title: Installation and Project Structure
section: Installing OpenTofu: Linux, macOS, Windows, and Containerized Options
text:
Installing OpenTofu: Linux, macOS, Windows, and Containerized Options
The worked path in this book is Linux, with the version selected by a runtime manager so the repository and the laptop agree.
Linux, pinned with mise. mise ships an OpenTofu backend. From the project directory:
mise use opentofu@1.13.2
mise exec -- tofu version
A global install is mise use -g opentofu@1.13.2. The project file mise writes belongs in git. A laptop without mise can install the same release from the official installer, which also configures the project’s apt or rpm repository:
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL \
  https://get.opentofu.org/install-opentofu.sh -o install-opentofu.sh
chmod +x install-opentofu.sh
./install-opentofu.sh --install-method deb
--install-method rpm is the dnf/yum equivalent. The package name is tofu. An apt repository that tracks “latest” will walk off 1.13 the day 1.14 ships. A pin beats a floating distro package for this book.
macOS. Homebrew’s brew install opentofu is the OpenTofu tap and tracks current. For 1.13.2 specifically, use mise or the release tarball. 1.13 requires macOS 13 or newer. Official 32-bit builds are gone.
Windows. Install the signed 1.13.2 package from the OpenTofu GitHub release, or the OpenTofu package in winget, and confirm the version in the next section. Windows on ARM64 is supported in 1.13. There is no official 32-bit build. WinRM provisioners are gone in this series. Use OpenSSH if a provisioner must reach Windows, and prefer not to use a provisioner at all (chapter 10).
Containers. The project publishes images at ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu. Pin the tag:
docker run --rm ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu:1.13.2 version
Mount the working directory when you init or plan. latest is not a pin. The minimal tag is the one to copy a binary out of when you build your own image.

title: Installation and Project Structure
section: Verifying Your Installation and Checking Versions
text:
Verifying Your Installation and Checking Versions
tofu version prints the release and the platform. You want 1.13.2 on the platform you will apply from. A plan created on 1.13.2 should be applied by 1.13.2. Providers have their own versions, printed by tofu version after init and locked in .terraform.lock.hcl.
Three versions are in play, and mixing them up wastes an afternoon:








Version
Where it lives
What breaks if it floats




OpenTofu
tofu version, .terraform-version, mise
Language and state behaviour


Provider
required_providers and the lock file
Arguments the resource accepts


Module
source and version on a module block
Inputs the child expects



required_version = "~> 1.13.0" refuses to run on 1.12 and on 1.14. That pessimism is correct for a book pin. Widen it only when you have read the changelog.

title: Installation and Project Structure
section: The Minimal Working Project
text:
The Minimal Working Project
Create a directory with one file, main.tf, containing the random_pet configuration from chapter 2. Then:
tofu init
tofu plan -out=tfplan
tofu apply tfplan
tofu output name
Init creates .terraform/ and .terraform.lock.hcl. Plan writes a binary plan. Apply updates terraform.tfstate. Output prints the pet name. A second tofu plan should report no changes.
Delete the experiment with tofu destroy when you are done with it. The state file is not a secret worth keeping for a pet name, and it is a secret-shaped file the moment a real resource lands in it.

title: Installation and Project Structure
section: Directory Layout Conventions: Single Project vs. Modular Organization
text:
Directory Layout Conventions: Single Project vs. Modular Organization
A single project is one root module: the directory where you run tofu.
network/
├── main.tf            # resources, or a thin file that calls modules
├── variables.tf       # input variables
├── outputs.tf         # outputs
├── versions.tf        # required_version and required_providers
├── providers.tf       # provider configuration
├── terraform.tfvars   # values for this environment, if not secret
├── .terraform.lock.hcl
└── .terraform-version
Filenames are convention. OpenTofu loads every .tf and .tofu file in the directory and ignores the names. The split exists so a reviewer knows where to look.
A modular organisation pulls reusable blocks into child modules (chapter 8) and keeps each environment or each account as its own root module with its own state. That is the layout chapter 14 uses for production. Start in one directory until the pet example is boring. Splitting early hides the tool behind a forest of folders.

section: Configuration File Naming Rules: main.tf, variables.tf, and Beyond

Configuration File Naming Rules: main.tf, variables.tf, and Beyond







File
Put it here




versions.tf
terraform block: version, providers, backend, encryption

JSON (.tf.json) is valid and a poor authoring format. Generate HCL, or generate JSON from a tool and review the diff. Hand-written JSON configurations rot.

title: Installation and Project Structure
section: .terraform-version, .gitignore, and Essential Project Files
text:
.terraform-version, .gitignore, and Essential Project Files
.terraform-version contains 1.13.2. tfenv, tofuenv, and tenv read it. mise users can rely on mise.toml instead. One pin, not both, unless you have checked they agree.
Commit:

*.tf, *.tofu, *.tfvars that hold no secrets
.terraform.lock.hcl
.terraform-version or mise.toml
A README with the init/plan/apply commands

Never commit:

.terraform/ (provider binaries)
terraform.tfstate and terraform.tfstate.backup
*.tfplan and tfplan (plans can contain sensitive values)
crash.log
*.auto.tfvars or secret.auto.tfvars if they hold credentials
.terraformrc when it contains tokens

A .gitignore that encodes that list belongs in the first commit, before the first apply. The expensive mistake is committing a state file once. History keeps it after you delete the working copy.
TF_VAR_name environment variables fill variable name. Prefer them for secrets. Chapter 12 is the full rule. Chapter 5 is how variables are declared so that path works.

title: HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
text:
HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
HCL is a small language with a few traps that show up as a plan that cannot be computed. This chapter is the syntax you need to read anyone else’s module.

title: HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Parse a block into type, labels, and arguments
Choose a type instead of stringifying everything
Write a for expression and a dynamic block when repetition is data
Predict what null and an unknown value will do to count

title: HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
section: Blocks, Arguments, Comments, and Basic Structure
text:
Blocks, Arguments, Comments, and Basic Structure
A block has a type, zero or more labels, and a body.
resource "random_pet" "service" {
  length    = 2
  separator = "-"
}
resource is the type. "random_pet" and "service" are labels. length and separator are arguments. Argument order does not matter. A missing required argument is an error at plan time. An unknown argument is also an error, which is how typos die early.
# and // comment to end of line. /* */ comments a range. Comments are not documentation the registry renders. Prefer a description on variables and outputs for anything a caller must see.
Identifiers are letters, digits, underscores, and hyphens in some positions. Resource local names should be stable. Renaming service to api is a new address, and state will want to destroy the old one.

title: HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
section: Attributes and Types: Strings, Numbers, Booleans, Lists, Maps, Objects
text:
Attributes and Types: Strings, Numbers, Booleans, Lists, Maps, Objects








Type
Literal
Use




string
"api"
Names, ids you were given


number
2
Counts and sizes. Do not quote numbers you intend to do arithmetic on


bool
true
Flags. The strings "true" and "false" are strings


list
["a", "b"]
Ordered, one element type in simple declarations


set
toset(["a", "a"])
Unordered, unique. A set of strings is the natural for_each


map
{ env = "prod" }
String keys, one value type


object
{ name = "api", port = 443 }
Named attributes with their own types


tuple
["api", 443]
Fixed positions, mixed types



A list and a tuple both use []. The type constraint you declare is what makes them different. Chapter 5’s variable types are these same types with validation on top.
Heredocs (<<-EOT … EOT) are strings. The closing marker sits at the left margin unless you use the dashed form, which strips the indentation of the least-indented line.

title: HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
section: Expressions: Interpolation, Conditionals, and Operators
text:
Expressions: Interpolation, Conditionals, and Operators
Inside strings, ${...} interpolates. "pet-${random_pet.service.id}" is a string. Outside strings, you do not wrap references in quotes or in ${}. random_pet.service.id is the value. "random_pet.service.id" is the text of that address and a classic bug.
Conditionals are condition ? then_value : else_value. Both branches are typed together. A branch that returns a string and a branch that returns a number will fail or coerce in a way you will not like. Make them the same type.
&&, ||, and ! are boolean. +, -, *, / are numeric. == and != compare. Comparisons against null are how optional values show up. Operator precedence will surprise you less if you parenthesise the conditional.
A splat aws_instance.web[*].id turns a list of resources into a list of attributes. On a resource that uses for_each, the value is a map, and you want a for expression rather than a splat.

title: HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
section: Null, Unknown, and Type Conversion: Gotchas Every Engineer Must Know
text:
Null, Unknown, and Type Conversion: Gotchas Every Engineer Must Know
null means “omit this argument” for many optional resource arguments. It does not mean empty string, and it does not mean zero. A default of "" still sets the argument. A default of null leaves it unset so the provider can apply its own default. Those produce different plans.
An unknown value is a value that will exist only after apply: the id of a resource being created in this same plan. Unknown values flow through expressions. They poison anything that must be decided during the plan, especially count and for_each. You cannot yet know how many instances to plan if the count depends on an id that does not exist.
OpenTofu 1.13 adds two functions aimed at that wall, still settling toward a stable design in 1.14. convert asks the planner to treat an unknown as a given type. assumenotnull tells the planner a value will not be null. If apply later violates the hint, OpenTofu errors instead of silently doing something else. Use them at a module boundary when a caller passes a value the plan cannot see through. Do not use them to paper over a count that should have been a static map.
tostring, tonumber, tolist, and tomap coerce explicitly. Implicit coercion of a bool to a string is how a tag set becomes "true" in one environment and true in another. Coerce at the edge.
try(expr, fallback) catches errors in expressions. It also catches typos. Prefer a type constraint over try when the failure is a mistake you want to see.

title: HCL Syntax and Language Fundamentals
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Blocks have a type, labels, and arguments. Names of files do not change that
Unquoted references are values. Quoted references are strings
for builds collections. dynamic builds nested blocks. Stable keys keep state stable
null unsets an optional argument. Unknown values cannot size count
1.13’s convert and assumenotnull are hints to the planner, checked again at apply

title: Variables, Locals, and Outputs
text:
Variables, Locals, and Outputs
Variables are the module’s arguments. Locals are its private names. Outputs are the only values a parent should read. This chapter is that contract.

title: Variables, Locals, and Outputs
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Declare a variable with a type, a default, and a validation

Variable Files (.tfvars): Environment-Specific Configuration Management
terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars load automatically. Any other name loads with -var-file=prod.tfvars. A variable file is assignment, not logic:
pet_length = 3
Typical layout once you have more than one environment: a root module per environment, each with its own backend and a small tfvars file, rather than one root module and a pile of var-files you forget to pass. Chapter 9 explains why workspaces are a weak substitute for that split. Chapter 14 draws the directories.
Precedence, from lowest to highest: defaults, environment variables TF_VAR_pet_length, terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars in name order, -var-file, -var. A value supplied later wins. In automation, pass -var-file explicitly so the file you reviewed is the file that ran. Do not rely on an auto.tfvars nobody mentioned in the pipeline.
Secrets do not go in a tfvars file that is committed. TF_VAR_state_passphrase from the pipeline’s secret store is the ordinary path. A local secret.auto.tfvars that is gitignored works on a laptop and will eventually be copied into a ticket. Prefer the environment.

title: Providers, Resources, and Data Sources in Depth
text:
Providers, Resources, and Data Sources in Depth
A provider is a plugin with credentials. A resource is one object that plugin owns on your behalf. A data source is a question. This chapter is how those three show up for AWS, Azure, and GCP, and how you stop a floating provider version from rewriting the plan.

title: Providers, Resources, and Data Sources in Depth

text:
Learning goals

Configure a provider without putting a long-lived key in the configuration
Read a resource schema as required, optional, computed, or deprecated
Write a small sketch for each of the three large clouds

section: Resource Arguments: Required, Optional, Computed, and Deprecated
text:
Resource Arguments: Required, Optional, Computed, and Deprecated
The provider schema, not this book, decides which arguments exist. The categories are stable:








Kind
In configuration
In state after apply




Required
You must set it
Stored


Optional
You may set it. Null usually means “leave the provider default”
Stored if set


Computed
You cannot set it, or you can set a related optional and the provider may override
Filled in by the provider


Optional and computed
If you set it, it is yours. If you do not, the provider chooses and stores the choice
The next plan may want to adopt the provider’s value



Computed-only attributes (an instance id, a bucket domain name) are outputs of the create call. Referencing them in the same plan is fine. Using them as a for_each key is the unknown-value problem from chapter 4.
Deprecated arguments still work until a provider major version removes them. A plan that warns is a plan you schedule a follow-up for. Ignoring deprecations is how a provider bump becomes a rewrite. Pin the provider, read the changelog at the bump, and do not combine a provider major bump with an OpenTofu minor bump in the same change.

text:
Version Constraints: Pinning Providers for Stability
The constraint in required_providers is a range. The lock file is the selected build.







Constraint
Meaning




= 5.70.0
This build only. Heavy for a library module, right for a root you do not want surprised


~> 5.70
Any 5.70.z. A reasonable root-module pin


~> 5.0
Any 5.x. Fine for a reusable module that promises compatibility. Loose for a root


>= 5.0.0
Anything newer, including 6.0.0, which may break. Avoid in roots



Commit .terraform.lock.hcl. A pipeline that runs tofu init -upgrade on every apply will take provider upgrades you did not review. Init without -upgrade uses the lock. Upgrade in a commit whose diff is the lock file and a plan you read.
Provider major versions are allowed to change arguments and to force resource replacement. Schedule them. The OpenTofu pin and the provider pin move in separate commits so a bad plan has one cause.

text:
Summary

Providers are plugins. Credentials come from the environment, not from the .tf file
Required, optional, and computed describe who is allowed to set an argument
AWS, Azure, and GCP sketches share a shape: explicit name, no embedded secret, owned by this state
Data sources read objects this state does not own
Aliases are extra configurations you pass into modules on purpose
The lock file is the pin. The constraint is only the allowed range

title: State Management and Backends
text:
State Management and Backends
State is the memory of object ids. A backend is where that memory lives and how it is locked. This chapter moves the pet example’s local file to a design you can hand to a second operator.

title: State Management and Backends
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Say what a state file stores, including values marked sensitive
Configure a remote backend with a lock
Read another project’s outputs without reading its resources
Move a state between backends, and recover from a lock that outlived its apply

title: State Management and Backends
section: Understanding State: What It Stores and Why Local Is Not Enough
text:
Understanding State: What It Stores and Why Local Is Not Enough
terraform.tfstate is JSON. For each resource address it stores the provider, the type, the id the provider returned, and the attributes from the last refresh. It also stores outputs and a serial number. Sensitive values are stored in full. The sensitive flag changes the CLI, not the file.
Local state fails as soon as two actors exist. Two engineers, or an engineer and a pipeline, apply two copies and each believes it owns the objects. The second apply creates duplicates or destroys the first world’s objects because they are absent from the second state. A laptop disk is also a poor backup.
Local state is still correct for a throwaway directory and for learning the commands. The moment the objects cost money or someone else must change them, the state moves.

title: State Management and Backends
section: Backend Types: Local, S3, Azure Blob, GCS, Consul, and More
text:
Backend Types: Local, S3, Azure Blob, GCS, Consul, and More
A backend is declared inside the terraform block. It is read at init, and changing it means tofu init -migrate-state or a fresh init, not a normal plan.








Backend
Typical use
Locking




local
Learning, throwaway
None that helps a team


s3
AWS accounts
From OpenTofu 1.10, a lock file in the bucket (use_lockfile = true). Older setups use a DynamoDB table


azurerm
Azure
Blob lease


gcs
Google Cloud
Object generation / lock in the bucket


consul
Environments that already run Consul
Session lock


http, pg, and others
When the platform standard is something else
Only if that backend implements it. A backend without a lock is a hazard



Pick the backend that sits next to the account you are managing, so the failure domains match a story you can tell: the AWS state lives in an AWS account dedicated to state, not in the same bucket the configuration is free to delete. Access to the state backend is access to every secret the state holds and to the power to unlock or overwrite it. Chapter 12 narrows that IAM.
An example shape for S3, not a bucket this book creates for you:
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "example-tofu-state"
    key          = "pets/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
encrypt = true is server-side encryption at the bucket. It is not OpenTofu’s client-side encryption. You can use both. Client-side encryption is the encryption block below. Backend blocks cannot use variables or locals in older OpenTofu. Since 1.8 they can, which is useful and also a way to point production at the wrong bucket with a typo in a local. Prefer a partial backend config (tofu init -backend-config=backend.hcl) for the key and bucket, so the committed configuration does not contain an account-specific name you copy between environments by accident.

title: State Management and Backends
section: State Migration: Moving Between Backends Safely
text:
State Migration: Moving Between Backends Safely
Changing the backend block and running tofu init -migrate-state copies state from the old backend to the new one and offers to delete the old copy. Do this with a lock, with a fresh backup of the source state, and with nobody else applying.
The safe sequence:

Stop pipelines that apply this state
tofu state pull > backup.tfstate and store that file somewhere encrypted, not in git
Change the backend configuration in a review
tofu init -migrate-state
tofu plan and confirm the plan is empty
Re-enable pipelines pointed at the new backend
Only then delete the backup, after the retention window you promised yourself

tofu state mv moves an address inside one state, or between states with pull and push. Renaming a resource without moved or state mv destroys and recreates. A moved block in the configuration is the reviewable form:
moved {
  from = random_pet.service
  to   = random_pet.api
}
Leave the block in place through one release so every state has applied it, then remove it.

title: State Management and Backends
section: State Troubleshooting: Corruption, Drift, and Recovery Procedures
text:
State Troubleshooting: Corruption, Drift, and Recovery Procedures
A stale lock. The apply died and the lock remains. Read the lock. If the id matches a dead run and no apply is in progress, tofu force-unlock LOCK_ID removes it. Unlocking a live apply is how two writers corrupt state. Look at the pipeline before you unlock.
Drift. tofu plan shows a change you did not make. Either the console edit is wrong and you apply to put the object back, or the console edit is the new truth and you import it into configuration. Refresh-only (tofu apply -refresh-only) updates state to match the world without changing the world. Use it when you have decided the world is right and the state is stale. Do not use it as a weekly habit to hide drift you should have configured.
A corrupt or empty state. Stop. Restore the previous version from the backend’s object versioning, or from the backup you pulled. tofu state push replaces remote state with a file you have inspected. Pushing the wrong file is a worse incident than the one you were fixing. Inspect with tofu show -json backup.tfstate and confirm resource addresses before you push.
Resources in state and not in configuration. The next apply destroys them. That is either the change you wanted or an accidental deletion of a .tf file. Read a destroy plan from the bottom. terraform.tfstate.backup on a local backend is a single generation. It is not a history.
Never edit state JSON by hand unless you are following a documented recovery and you have a copy of the previous bytes. The CLI subcommands (state rm, state mv, import, force-unlock) exist so the serial number and the checksum stay consistent.
