text:
Summary

State stores ids and attributes, including sensitive ones, in full
A remote backend with a lock and versioning is the minimum for two operators
Server-side encryption and OpenTofu’s client-side encryption solve different problems. Production can use both
Remote state consumers depend on outputs only
Migrate with a backup, an empty plan, and pipelines paused
Unlock only a dead lock. Restore state from a version, do not hand-edit it

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
text:
Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
A module is a directory of configuration that can be called with inputs and returns outputs. The root module is the one you apply. Everything else is a child. This chapter is how to draw that line so a module stays reusable without becoming a second programming language.

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Call a local child module and read its outputs
Decide what belongs inside the module and what stays in the root
Pin a registry or git source the way you pin a provider
Recognise a module that hides too much

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: What Is a Module?: Root Modules, Child Modules, and Published Modules
text:
What Is a Module?: Root Modules, Child Modules, and Published Modules
Every directory you run tofu in is a root module. It has the backend, the provider configuration, and the state. A child module is a directory you refer to with a module block. It has variables, resources, and outputs. It does not have its own backend. Its resources live in the root’s state, under addresses like module.pets.random_pet.service.
A published module is a child someone else versions. The OpenTofu registry, a git tag, or an OCI artifact are sources. Publishing does not change the language. It changes who is allowed to move the inputs under you.
One root module per state remains the rule. A child that tries to configure a backend is ignored or rejected. If two parts of the system must change on different schedules or different permissions, they are two roots, not two children.

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: Designing Your First Module: Inputs, Outputs, and Responsibility Boundaries
text:
Designing Your First Module: Inputs, Outputs, and Responsibility Boundaries
A module does one thing a caller can name: “a pet name with a prefix”, “a bucket with versioning and a policy”, “a network with these subnets”. If the name needs “and”, it is probably two modules.
modules/pets/
├── versions.tf
├── variables.tf
├── main.tf
└── outputs.tf
# modules/pets/variables.tf
variable "pet_length" {
  type    = number
  default = 2
}

# modules/pets/main.tf
resource "random_pet" "service" {
  length = var.pet_length
}

# modules/pets/outputs.tf
output "name" {
  value = random_pet.service.id
}
The boundary test: a caller who does not care how you implemented it should still be able to use it. If the caller must know you used random_pet, the output is leaking the implementation and the module is a folder pretending to be an API. Export the name. Keep the resource type inside.
Do not put provider credentials in a child. The root configures providers and passes aliases. Do not put environment names inside the module as a switch (if var.env == "prod"). Pass the values that differ. A module that contains a production special case is a root module that cannot be reused.

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: Calling Modules: Local Paths, Registry Sources, and Git Repositories

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: The OpenTofu Registry: Publishing and Consuming Community Modules
text:
The OpenTofu Registry: Publishing and Consuming Community Modules
registry.opentofu.org serves provider and module metadata. Consuming a module is the source and version above, then tofu init. The registry records who published the module. That namespace is the identity you are trusting, the same way a provider namespace is.
Publishing is a review, not an upload button hidden in the CLI. The registry project accepts modules through its documented submission process. A module you publish is a contract: input types, outputs, and the objects you create. A breaking change is a major version. Yanking a version that someone has pinned breaks their init. Do not republish a tag with different code.
Prefer a small number of modules your team owns over a deep tree of community modules you have not read. A community module that creates IAM is a module you read line by line before the first apply. Fork and pin if you depend on it and you cannot accept surprise commits.

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: Advanced Module Patterns: Stacks, Composition, and Versioned Releases

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: Anti-Patterns: Monolithic Modules, Hidden Dependencies, and Over-Abstraction
text:
Anti-Patterns: Monolithic Modules, Hidden Dependencies, and Over-Abstraction
The monolith. One module creates the network, the cluster, the database, and the DNS. Every change plans everything. Split along change rate and along ownership.
Hidden dependencies. A module looks up a VPC by tag inside a data source the caller did not pass. The caller cannot see the dependency. Pass the VPC id in. The plan then shows where it came from.
Over-abstraction. A “universal cloud instance” module with var.cloud and three implementations is three modules and a switch that fails in the ways all three clouds fail. Write the AWS module and the Azure module. Share a naming local if you must. Do not share a resource graph that does not exist.
Pass-through variables. A child variable that exists only to be passed to a grandchild, unchanged, with no default and no validation, means the middle module has no opinion. Delete the middle module.
Defaults that create cost. A default of true on “create a NAT gateway per zone” surprises a caller in a lab account. Defaults should be the safe, small choice. Production opts in.

title: Modules: Building Reusable Infrastructure Components
section: Summary
text:
Summary

The root owns the backend and the state. Children own a reusable graph
Inputs and outputs are the API. Resource addresses are not
Pin registry versions and git refs. A branch is not a pin
Compose a few modules at the root. Do not build a framework
A module that looks up its own dependencies hides the thing the plan should show

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
text:
Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
These are the controls that change what a plan is allowed to do: which state you are in, whether a resource may be destroyed, and which edges the graph waits for. They are also easy to use as a substitute for a layout you should have drawn in chapter 14.

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Explain a workspace as a separate state, not a separate configuration
Decide when a workspace is the wrong environment boundary
Set create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, and ignore_changes for a reason
Read a dependency graph and force replacement without editing the cloud by hand

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: Workspaces: Multiple Environments from One Configuration
text:
Workspaces: Multiple Environments from One Configuration
A workspace is a named state inside one backend, selected with tofu workspace select. The configuration does not change when you switch. terraform.workspace (the name of the value, kept for compatibility) is a string you can interpolate, usually into names.
resource "random_pet" "service" {
  length = 2
  prefix = terraform.workspace
}
default exists even when you have never created another workspace. tofu workspace new staging makes a second state. Apply in staging does not update default. That isolation is the feature.
The CLI remembers the selected workspace in local files. A pipeline must select the workspace explicitly (tofu workspace select production) and fail if the select fails. An apply that runs in default because the select was skipped is an apply into the wrong state.

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: When Workspaces Help (and When They Hurt): Practical Guidance
text:
When Workspaces Help (and When They Hurt): Practical Guidance
Workspaces help when the environments are the same shape, the same permissions boundary, and the same blast radius: a developer sandbox per person, or a short-lived test state. They hurt when production and development differ in account, credentials, or who is allowed to apply.
Production state in the same backend configuration as development, separated only by a workspace name, means a missed workspace select can plan against production with development credentials or the reverse. Separate root modules, separate backend keys, and separate pipelines make that mistake a file you did not mean to enter rather than a flag you forgot.
Do not use the workspace name as the only difference in a large conditional (terraform.workspace == "production" ? big : small) that changes counts and providers. That configuration cannot be read without knowing which state it will meet. Two directories that call the same child module with different variables are longer and clearer.
If you already have workspaces and they are small, keep them until the permission boundary appears. Do not migrate in the middle of an incident.

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: Lifecycle Arguments: create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: Dependency Management: Explicit depends_on vs. Implicit References
text:
Dependency Management: Explicit depends_on vs. Implicit References
A reference is a dependency. If module.record takes module.name.name, the record waits for the name. You do not add depends_on for that edge. The graph already has it.
depends_on is for edges the configuration cannot see: a data source that reads an object created in the same apply, or a provisioner-shaped side effect you have not yet removed. Every explicit edge is a serialisation. A module-level depends_on waits for the entire module, which is coarser than waiting for one output and can slow the plan’s apply for no gain.
Do not depends_on a resource to paper over a missing attribute reference. Pass the attribute. The next reader can then see why the order exists.
Cycles are errors. A cycle means two objects each need the other’s id. Break it by creating one of them with a name you already know, or by splitting the states. A cycle is a design signal, not a flag to relax.

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: The Dependency Graph: Visualizing and Debugging Execution Order
text:
The Dependency Graph: Visualizing and Debugging Execution Order
tofu graph prints a DOT graph of the addresses and their edges. Render it when you do not believe the order an apply is taking. Most of the time the plan’s explanation of a replacement is enough and the full graph is noise.
What you are looking for:

An edge you did not intend, usually from a reference used only in a tag
A missing edge, usually a data source that reads too early
A module that everything depends on because its outputs are a grab-bag

tofu apply -target=random_pet.service applies only that node and what it requires. Targeting is a recovery tool. An apply that always targets has left the declarative model, and the untargeted objects drift from the configuration without anyone noticing. Follow a targeted apply with a full plan the same day.

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: Tainting Resources: Forcing Recreation When Needed
text:
Tainting Resources: Forcing Recreation When Needed
Tainting marks an object so the next plan replaces it, even though the configuration did not change. The modern form is:
tofu apply -replace=random_pet.service
-replace is the flag to use. The older tofu taint still exists and is easier to forget in state. Replacement runs the destroy and create according to create_before_destroy and the graph. For the pet resource that only changes a name. For a database it deletes data. Read the plan.
Replace when the object is wrong in a way the configuration cannot express: a virtual machine whose user-data ran once and failed, a secret that was issued and must be reissued. Do not replace as a substitute for understanding a drift. If the configuration is wrong, fix the configuration. If the world is wrong and the configuration is right, replace.

title: Workspaces, Lifecycle Rules, and Dependencies
section: Summary
text:
Summary

A workspace is another state for the same configuration. Select it explicitly
Separate roots when accounts, credentials, or blast radius differ
prevent_destroy and create_before_destroy are promises about replacement. ignore_changes is a list, not all
References build the graph. depends_on is for edges a reference cannot see
-replace forces recreation. -target is a recovery hatch followed by a full plan

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
text:
Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
Provisioners run a script against a resource after OpenTofu has created it. Import does the opposite kind of work: it tells state about an object that already exists. One of these belongs in a modern module. This chapter is how to tell them apart, and how to bring a legacy object under management without recreating it.

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Explain why a provisioner breaks the declarative model
Name the few cases where local-exec is still honest
Import an existing object and generate configuration for it
Plan a migration that ends with OpenTofu as the owner

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: The Problem With Provisioners: Why They Are Discouraged
text:
The Problem With Provisioners: Why They Are Discouraged
A resource argument is stored in state and corrected on the next plan. A provisioner runs and is forgotten. The script’s effect is invisible to the next plan unless the script’s failure happened to fail the apply. The object looks clean while the package the script installed has drifted.
Provisioners also put an imperative tool inside a declarative run: SSH keys, WinRM (removed from OpenTofu 1.13’s file and remote-exec), a shell on the machine running tofu. That shell has the pipeline’s credentials. A local-exec that curl-posts to an API is a second provider with none of the provider’s diff.
The replacements are ordinary provider features. Cloud-init and user-data are arguments. Configuration management is a tool that converges on its own. A Kubernetes manifest is a resource of its provider. An API call you need every time is a provider resource, even if you have to write a small one. Reach for a provisioner only after those options are genuinely absent.

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: When Provisioners Make Sense: file, local-exec, remote-exec, and Beyond
text:
When Provisioners Make Sense: file, local-exec, remote-exec, and Beyond
local-exec runs on the machine where tofu runs. The honest uses are narrow: call a control-plane API the provider does not cover yet, during a migration you have dated; or render a one-shot artifact the provider cannot. Even then, a null resource with a local-exec is a resource whose only behaviour is the script, and it will not re-run when the script’s inputs change unless you wire a trigger.
file and remote-exec copy and run on the new machine over SSH. They need a connection block, a reachable address, and a key. They fail when the network path from the pipeline to the instance does not exist, which is the common production case. In 1.13 they do not speak WinRM. If the instance is Windows, use a different channel or, better, an image that does not need a post-create script.
creation-time provisioners run on create. destroy-time provisioners run before destroy. A destroy-time provisioner that must succeed or it blocks destruction will block an incident. Prefer the provider’s own deletion behaviour.
There is no “beyond” that makes provisioners a design. Chef and Puppet provisioner bridges were the old pattern. Leave them in the history of the module you are migrating.

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: Best Practices If You Must Use Provisioners: Idempotency and Error Handling
text:
Best Practices If You Must Use Provisioners: Idempotency and Error Handling
If a migration still has one:

Make the script idempotent. Running it twice converges. A script that appends a line every time is not finished
Fail the script with a non-zero status. A provisioner that swallows errors reports a successful apply
Pass data as arguments or environment, not as a string interpolated into a shell command you did not quote
Trigger replacement or re-run from a hash of the inputs, or accept that the script runs only on create and document that
Keep the script in the repository, not on a laptop path
Delete the provisioner in a follow-up commit once the provider has the resource. Put that follow-up on the same change request

on_failure = continue hides the failure. Do not set it to get a green pipeline.

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: Importing Existing Resources: The import Command and Workflow

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: Generating Configuration for Imported Resources: State Inspection Techniques
text:
Generating Configuration for Imported Resources: State Inspection Techniques
tofu plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf writes HCL for addresses in import blocks that do not yet have configuration. The file is a starting point. It is not a module.
Generated configuration dumps every attribute the provider returned, including ones you should not set because they are computed, and ones that differ from the provider’s defaults in ways that will churn. Edit it down to the arguments you intend to own. Then plan again.
Inspection tools while you edit:



Command
What you learn




tofu state show aws_s3_bucket.state
Attributes currently stored


tofu state list
Addresses in this state


tofu show -json
The same facts for a script


A refresh-only plan
Whether the world and the state still agree



Do not generate configuration for an entire account in one pass. Import the object you mean to change, get an empty plan, and then import the next one. A generated file of hundreds of resources is a state you cannot review.

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: Migration Strategies: Bringing Legacy Infrastructure Under OpenTofu Control
text:
Migration Strategies: Bringing Legacy Infrastructure Under OpenTofu Control
A migration is a sequence of empty plans, not a flag day.

Inventory the objects and decide which ones OpenTofu will own. Some should stay outside: the state bucket itself is often created by hand or by a tiny bootstrap root so the backend exists before init
Write or generate configuration for one group that changes together
Import, plan, and stop when the plan is empty
Apply a no-op so state and configuration are known-good
Only then change an argument in a later commit
Remove the import blocks
Turn on prevent_destroy for objects the migration must not casually delete

Two teams must not manage the same object. If a console workflow still edits it, either stop that workflow or ignore_changes the specific argument and say why. Dual ownership is the drift you will be paged for.
Account-level tools that only scan and suggest imports are fine as a map. They are a poor author of the module boundary. You still decide what the root module is.
When the legacy object cannot be imported because the provider has no import for that type, you are stuck with a one-time recreation or with leaving it unmanaged. Recreate only when you can afford the replacement. Write that down. A provisioner is not the bridge across a missing import.

title: Provisioners and Importing Existing Infrastructure
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Provisioners run and forget. Resource arguments are corrected on the next plan
OpenTofu 1.13’s file and remote-exec provisioners do not speak WinRM
If a script remains, it is idempotent, it fails loudly, and it has a removal date
Import with a reviewed import block, then edit configuration until the plan is empty
Generated HCL is a draft. Migrate one group at a time, and do not share ownership with the console

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
text:
Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
A plan a human reads is the most important test. The commands in this chapter exist so that human never has to spend the review on indentation, a missing variable, or a security group open to the world. Sentinel is not one of those commands on OpenTofu.

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Run tofu fmt and tofu validate as a gate, not as a suggestion
Write a tofu test that fails when the pet length drifts
Put policy in Open Policy Agent, not in Sentinel
Scan configuration with Checkov or Trivy before the plan is the first time someone notices

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: Formatting and Linting: tofu fmt, tofu validate, and Custom Rules
text:
Formatting and Linting: tofu fmt, tofu validate, and Custom Rules
tofu fmt -recursive rewrites files to the canonical layout. tofu fmt -check -recursive exits non-zero when it would have changed something. The check belongs in the pipeline. The rewrite belongs in a pre-commit hook so the pipeline almost never sees a format failure.
tofu validate loads the configuration, checks syntax, and checks that references and types line up. It does not call providers. A directory that has not been initialised can validate only partway. In CI, init with -backend=false so validate can see the providers without needing state credentials, then validate.
tofu fmt -check -recursive
tofu init -backend=false
tofu validate
Custom rules beyond the language are policy, covered below. A linter that reimplements the type system is redundant with validate. A linter that encodes “buckets must have versioning” is policy and should live where policy lives.
OpenTofu 1.13 includes early built-in lint work. Treat it as an extra signal in this series, and keep fmt and validate as the gates you require. Do not fail a production pipeline on an experimental lint until you have read what it considers an error.

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: Pre-commit Hooks: Catching Errors Before They Reach the Repository
text:
Pre-commit Hooks: Catching Errors Before They Reach the Repository
A pre-commit hook runs fmt and validate on the directories the commit touches. Keep the hook fast. Provider downloads inside a hook are how people start skipping the hook.
The hook is a convenience. The pipeline runs the same commands. A skipped hook must not be the only place a check existed. Document the hook as a one-line install in the repository README, and make the CI job the authority.
Useful extra checks in the same hook: reject a commit that adds terraform.tfstate, reject *.tfplan, and reject a file that looks like a cloud access key. Those are secret checks, not format checks. Chapter 12 lists the patterns.

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: Testing Strategies: Unit Tests, Integration Tests, and Plan Validation
text:
Testing Strategies: Unit Tests, Integration Tests, and Plan Validation
Three layers, cheapest first.
Static. fmt, validate, policy, and a scanner. No credentials. Every pull request.
Plan tests. tofu test with command = plan asserts on values the plan can know: names, counts, policy documents built from locals. The random provider is enough for the pet module. No cloud account.
Apply tests. command = apply creates real objects and destroys them at the end of the test. Run these in an account built for tests, with a budget and a janitor. They do not run on every keystroke. They run on the module when its contract changes, and nightly if you can afford the time.
A plan a reviewer reads is still required for production roots. Tests do not replace that review. They make the review about the infrastructure change rather than about a typo.

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: OpenTofu Test Framework: Built-in Testing Capabilities

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: Policy as Code: Sentinel, OPA, and openpolicyagent Integration
text:
Policy as Code: Sentinel, OPA, and openpolicyagent Integration
Sentinel is HashiCorp’s policy language, enforced in their commercial Terraform platform. OpenTofu does not run Sentinel. A .sentinel policy pack will not gate tofu apply. If a migration guide tells you to point Sentinel at OpenTofu, it is describing the other product.
Open Policy Agent is the policy tool that fits. You evaluate a plan JSON or a configuration JSON with a Rego policy. Conftest is a small runner around that. The usual place is CI, after tofu plan -out=tfplan and tofu show -json tfplan > plan.json.
tofu plan -out=tfplan
tofu show -json tfplan > plan.json
conftest test plan.json --policy policy/
A policy that denies 0.0.0.0/0 on a security group, or denies a resource type the team has banned, fails the job before apply. Write Rego against the plan JSON’s resource changes, not against a cloud API. The plan is what you are about to do.
Keep policies in a repository the infrastructure repositories consume at a pinned version. A policy copied into each repo will be edited in one of them during an incident and will never return. An exception is a reviewed waiver with an expiry, the same shape as any other break-glass.

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: Security Scanning: Detecting Misconfigurations with tfsec, checkov, and Trivy
text:
Security Scanning: Detecting Misconfigurations with tfsec, checkov, and Trivy
tfsec was a Terraform scanner. Its maintainers folded that work into Trivy. New pipelines should run Trivy or Checkov, not a frozen tfsec binary. The syllabus name is the history. The command you install is one of the living tools.
Both read configuration and look for misconfigurations: public buckets, open security groups, unencrypted disks. They do not replace policy you wrote, and they do not know your naming rules. Run one of them in CI so a well-known mistake fails without a custom Rego rule.
trivy config .
or:
checkov -d . --framework terraform
Checkov still says “terraform” for the framework name because the file format is the same. Point it at OpenTofu files. It does not need the Terraform binary.
Triage the first run. A hundred historical findings are not a gate. Turn the gate on for severity you will actually fix, and file the rest. A scanner that fails every build teaches people to ignore scanners. Pin the scanner version the same way you pin OpenTofu, so a rule change is a commit.

title: Testing, Validation, Formatting, and Policy Enforcement
section: Summary
text:
Summary

tofu fmt -check and tofu validate run in CI after tofu init -backend=false
Pre-commit is the fast path. The pipeline is the authority
tofu test asserts the module contract. Plan tests need no cloud
Sentinel does not run on OpenTofu. OPA/Conftest evaluates the plan JSON
Trivy config or Checkov catches known-bad configuration. tfsec’s rules live on in that lineage

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
text:
Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
OpenTofu’s privilege is the privilege of the credentials it holds, plus whoever can read the state. This chapter is how to keep both smaller than “the whole cloud.”

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Encrypt state in transit and at rest, including client-side encryption
Authenticate providers with roles, not with long-lived keys in files
Scope the apply role to the resources this root manages
Notice the audit record you do and do not get from tofu itself

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Securing State Files: Encryption at Rest and in Transit
text:
Securing State Files: Encryption at Rest and in Transit
State contains resource attributes. Those include generated passwords if a resource created one, access keys if a resource created one, and the raw values behind anything you marked sensitive. Assume the state is a secret store even when you tried not to put secrets in it.
Three different locks, and you want the ones that match the backend:







Control
What it actually does




TLS to the backend
Stops a network observer reading the state on the wire. The S3, Azure, and GCS backends use HTTPS


Server-side encryption
The bucket or account encrypts bytes at rest. encrypt = true on the S3 backend is this. Turn it on


Client-side encryption
OpenTofu encrypts before upload, so the cloud account stores ciphertext. The encryption block in chapter 7. enforced = true so a misconfiguration cannot write plaintext


Backend IAM
Who may GetObject and PutObject. This is the real access list


Versioning
Recovers from a bad write. It also retains old secrets until the versions expire. Expire on purpose



A local terraform.tfstate on a laptop is an unencrypted secret if the disk is not encrypted, and a stolen secret if the laptop is. Do not leave production state local “just for the migration” longer than that migration’s window.
Plans are state-shaped. tofu plan -out=tfplan writes sensitive values into the plan file. Delete it after apply. Do not archive plans in the build artifacts without the same encryption as state.

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Managing Secrets: Never Hardcoding Credentials
text:
Managing Secrets: Never Hardcoding Credentials
A credential in a .tf or .tfvars file will be committed, or copied into a plan log, or both. Patterns that hold up:

Provider credentials from the environment or from a workload identity, never from a variable that is stored in tfvars
Application secrets generated by a secrets manager resource, or written into the secrets manager by its own API, not interpolated into a user-data string that then lands in state in clear text
sensitive = true on the variable so logs redact it. Remember the flag is not encryption
Ephemeral values and write-only arguments, which OpenTofu 1.11 understands, when the provider offers them. A write-only argument is not stored back into state. Prefer it for a password the provider can accept that way
A secret that must be passed as a variable comes from TF_VAR_... injected by the pipeline for that job, and is not echoed

If a secret has already been committed, rotate it. Deleting the file in a follow-up commit does not remove it from history. Treat the old value as public.

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Provider Authentication Patterns: IAM Roles, Service Principals, Workload Identity
text:
Provider Authentication Patterns: IAM Roles, Service Principals, Workload Identity
The apply process assumes a role that exists only for that run.
AWS. A pipeline’s OIDC token assumes an IAM role. No static access key. Locally, a human assumes a role with a short session. The provider block stays region only.
Azure. Workload identity federation or a managed identity for the runner. A service principal with a client secret is the legacy path. If you still have the secret, it lives in the pipeline secret store and is injected as environment variables the azurerm provider already understands.
GCP. Workload identity federation from the pipeline, or the attached service account on the runner. GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS pointing at a JSON key on disk is the pattern to retire.
On-premises appliances. Use the provider’s token with the same rule: short-lived, injected, scoped to the device the root manages. A shared break-glass password in a provider block is how the network team and the OpenTofu state end up with the same god credential.
Humans and pipelines use different roles. A human role might plan in production and apply only in development. The pipeline role applies in production and cannot be assumed from a laptop. Chapter 13 is where that split sits in the workflow.

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Least Privilege for OpenTofu Execution: IAM Policies and RBAC
text:
Least Privilege for OpenTofu Execution: IAM Policies and RBAC
The apply role can create and destroy whatever the configuration mentions, and anything the provider does as a side effect of those calls. Scope it.

One role per root module, not one role for the whole company
Permissions for the resource types that root manages, in the accounts it manages
A separate, smaller permission set for state: read and write of one bucket prefix, plus the lock, and nothing else. The state role and the infrastructure role can be the same principal in a small team. They should still be two policies you can read
No permission to edit the state bucket’s own policy from the infrastructure role. Otherwise a bad plan can lock you out, or open the state
Plan in CI can often use the apply role if you accept that plan-time data sources run with apply power. Say so. A read-only plan role is better when data sources allow it, and some providers do not plan cleanly as read-only. Test that before you promise it

Review the role when the configuration gains a new resource type. A pipeline that applies with AdministratorAccess will work and will teach nothing about the blast radius.

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Audit Logging and Compliance: Tracking Who Changed What and When
text:
Audit Logging and Compliance: Tracking Who Changed What and When
OpenTofu writes a plan and a state serial. It is not an audit log. The audit log is the combination of:







Record
Question it answers




The git commit that changed the .tf
Who asked for the change, and what the text was


The pipeline run that applied a saved plan
Who approved, when, and which plan digest


Cloud audit logs (CloudTrail, Activity Log, Cloud Audit Logs)
Which API calls the role made


Backend access logs
Who read or wrote the state object


tofu show of the plan artifact, if you retain it under the state encryption rules
What the apply was predicted to do



Retain those where your compliance regime says to retain them. A chat message that says “I applied” is not a record. A pipeline that applies from a laptop using a shared user is not a record either.
State encryption does not remove the need for access logs. It changes what a stolen object reveals. Someone who can assume the apply role can still read the decrypted view by running tofu state pull with the key. Log that too if the backend and the KMS allow it.

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Common Security Pitfalls: Exposed Keys, Overly Permissive Policies, and Insecure Backends
text:
Common Security Pitfalls: Exposed Keys, Overly Permissive Policies, and Insecure Backends








Pitfall
What it looks like
The fix




A key in terraform.tfvars
The next commit, or a plan log
Environment or workload identity. Rotate the key that leaked


State in git
terraform.tfstate in the repository history
Backend, rotate anything the file held, purge history if the repo is shared


A public state bucket
The backend ACL or a policy of Principal: *
Block public access. Review who GetObject allows


No lock
Two applies, a corrupt serial
use_lockfile or the backend’s lock. Refuse to apply without it


enforced left off
One init writes plaintext and you do not notice
enforced = true after the migration


Apply with an admin role
A bad module creates a second admin
A role per root, reviewed when resources change


A plan file as a build artifact
The artifact store becomes a second state bucket
Encrypt or delete. Do not keep plans next to unrelated logs


Shared default workspace
The production apply runs wherever the CLI last sat
Separate roots, or an explicit workspace select that fails closed

title: Security Best Practices and Secrets Management
section: Summary
text:
Summary

State and plans hold secrets. TLS, server-side encryption, client-side encryption, and IAM are four different controls
Credentials come from a role the pipeline assumes. They are not file contents
One apply role per root, plus a tight state policy
Git, the pipeline, and cloud audit logs together are the audit trail. The CLI is not
A leaked key is rotated. It is not merely deleted in the next commit

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
text:
CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
The production habit is: a commit produces a plan, a human approves the plan, and tofu apply runs that plan file. This chapter is that pipeline on GitHub Actions, the same shape on other CI systems, and what GitOps does and does not mean for OpenTofu.

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Split plan and apply so the applied plan is the reviewed plan
Wire a GitHub Actions workflow that uses OpenTofu 1.13.2 and a role, not a key
Keep approval in front of apply
Say where Argo CD and Flux fit, and where they do not apply a .tf file

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: The Infrastructure Pipeline: Commit, Plan, Review, Apply
text:
The Infrastructure Pipeline: Commit, Plan, Review, Apply
One root module, one pipeline:

On a pull request: tofu fmt -check, tofu init -backend=false or init with read-only state credentials, tofu validate, scanner, tofu plan -out=tfplan. Comment the plan summary on the request
A human reads the plan. Destroy lines and IAM changes are the lines to read first
On merge to the branch that is allowed to apply: init with the real backend, plan again, apply the new plan, or apply a plan that was stored and hashed if your change-control rules require the exact bytes from the review
The job fails if the workspace, the backend key, or the OpenTofu version is not the one the repository pinned

Re-planning on merge is the common, honest default. The configuration that merges is the configuration you plan. A plan file saved from the pull request goes stale if main moved. If you must apply the exact reviewed bytes, merge by fast-forward only and apply the stored plan before anything else lands. Record the plan digest in the approval.
Never tofu apply -auto-approve on a pull request from a fork. Credentials available to untrusted diffs are credentials you have given away. The plan job on a fork can run without credentials when the module’s tests allow it, and the apply job runs only on the protected branch.

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: GitHub Actions Integration: Complete Workflow Examples
text:
GitHub Actions Integration: Complete Workflow Examples
Pin the tool. mise or the GitHub release action both work. This sketch uses the official setup style and OIDC to AWS. The role trust policy allows this repository’s protected environment, not every branch.
name: tofu
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: opentofu/setup-opentofu@v1
        with:
          tofu_version: 1.13.2
      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/tofu-plan-pets
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: tofu init
      - run: tofu plan -out=tfplan -no-color
        working-directory: roots/pets
Check the current major of opentofu/setup-opentofu and aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials when you copy this. Actions move. The pins that matter for the tool itself are tofu_version: 1.13.2 and the commit or tag of the action, which you set to a full SHA in a real repository so a tag cannot move under you.
Apply is a second job, needs: plan, if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main', with the environment production requiring reviewers. It runs tofu apply -auto-approve tfplan only when tfplan was produced in that same workflow by the merge commit. A pull request job stops at plan.
The pet root can use the plan job with no AWS step at all. Keep the cloud role off the toy.

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: GitLab CI, Jenkins, and Azure DevOps: Multi-Platform Pipeline Patterns
text:
GitLab CI, Jenkins, and Azure DevOps: Multi-Platform Pipeline Patterns
The platform changes. The stages do not.









Stage
GitLab CI
Jenkins
Azure DevOps




Pin
Image ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu:1.13.2
The same image, or a mise install in the agent
The same image


Identity
id_tokens and the cloud’s OIDC
Workload identity on the agent, not a stored access key
Service connection with federation


Plan
Merge request pipeline
PR build
PR validation


Approve
Protected environment, required approvals
Input step before the apply job
Environment check on the production stage


Apply
Main-branch job
Job after the input, on main
Stage with a condition on the main branch



Write the plan to the job log in a redacted form. tofu show tfplan respects sensitive values better than printing state. Store the plan file as an artifact only for the minutes between plan and apply, encrypted at rest by the CI system, and delete it.
A Jenkins agent that holds a static cloud key for every job is the pattern these pipelines exist to leave. One role per root, assumed for that job, shows up in CloudTrail as that role.

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: GitOps With OpenTofu: Declarative Deployment Using ArgoCD and Flux
text:
GitOps With OpenTofu: Declarative Deployment Using ArgoCD and Flux
GitOps means the git repository is the desired state, and a running process converges the world to it. For Kubernetes, Argo CD and Flux are that process. They apply manifests. They do not natively apply OpenTofu.
Three layouts are honest:

Pipeline GitOps. Git is the source. The CI system in the previous sections is the reconciler. This is the default for cloud accounts and for on-premises appliances. You do not need Argo CD to say you deploy from git
OpenTofu provisions the cluster, Flux or Argo CD provisions the workloads. The cluster’s state lives in an OpenTofu root. The workloads live in a git repository those controllers watch. The handoff is an output: a cluster endpoint and a place the controller is installed. Do not also manage the same Deployment with OpenTofu
A controller runs OpenTofu. Projects such as the tofu-controller (the OpenTofu-oriented descendant of Weave’s tf-controller) watch a git repository and run plan and apply from inside the cluster. That is GitOps in the strict sense. It belongs when the cluster is already the control plane you operate. It is an extra system to secure: the controller’s cloud role, the source repository it can read, and what it does without a human. Put the approval gate in front of it the same way you would in CI, or accept that merge equals apply and say so

Do not point Argo CD at a directory of .tf files and expect a plan. Do not run a second reconciler against a state the pipeline also applies.

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: Approval Gates and Change Management: Human Review in Automated Workflows
text:
Approval Gates and Change Management: Human Review in Automated Workflows
The gate is a protected environment or an explicit approval job between plan and apply. The approver sees the plan summary, the commit, and the OpenTofu version. The approver is not the only author of the change when the repository’s rules require two people. For a one-person lab, the gate can be you, and the pipeline still runs the apply so the laptop is not the only place with credentials.
Exceptions during an incident are a break-glass role that is logged and time-limited. The commit still lands. Applying from a laptop with the break-glass role and never pushing the configuration is how state and git diverge. Chapter 10’s import and chapter 7’s drift are the cleanup if that already happened.
Destructive plans need a louder gate: a second reviewer, or a rule that fails the job unless a label such as allow-destroy is present. Encode “this plan destroys” as a check on the plan JSON so it does not depend on someone scrolling.

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: Parallel Execution and Performance Optimization: Scaling Plans and Applies
text:
Parallel Execution and Performance Optimization: Scaling Plans and Applies
OpenTofu walks the graph and applies independent resources in parallel. -parallelism=n raises or lowers that fan-out. The default is enough until an API rate-limits you or a provider starts failing under load. Lower it before you raise it. A higher number does not fix a slow data source.
What actually speeds a large root:

Split roots along the seams in chapter 14 so one plan is not the entire company
Stop using depends_on on whole modules when an output reference is enough
Keep data sources off moving targets so plans are stable and caches are meaningful
Run tofu plan only in the roots the change touches. A monorepo of many roots does not plan all of them on every commit. Path filters do that
Init once per job and reuse the provider cache directory when the runner allows it. A cold init of every provider on every plan dominates small configurations

-refresh=false skips the refresh and plans against state only. It is faster and it is wrong when the world has drifted. Use it for a local syntax experiment, not for the production apply. There is a narrower “minimal refresh” idea on some Terraform lines. Do not assume the OpenTofu flag set matches Terraform 1.17. Check tofu plan -help on 1.13.2.
State locking already serialises applies of one root. Do not also serialise unrelated roots. They have different locks. Parallel pipelines across roots are safe. Parallel pipelines against one state are the lock doing its job: the second waits or fails.

title: CI/CD Integration, GitOps, and Automation Workflows
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Pull requests plan. The protected branch applies the plan it just created
Pin OpenTofu to 1.13.2 in the workflow. Assume a role. Do not store a cloud key
GitLab, Jenkins, and Azure DevOps use the same stages
Argo CD and Flux reconcile Kubernetes. A pipeline or a tofu controller reconciles OpenTofu
Approval sits between plan and apply. A destroy is a louder approval
Speed comes from smaller roots and fewer false edges, not from a larger parallelism number

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
text:
Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
Enterprise scale is not a bigger state file. It is a set of root modules with owners, a promotion path that does not rely on a workspace name, and an upgrade habit that reads changelogs. This chapter is that layout for cloud and on-premises together.

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Learning goals
text:
Learning goals

Split accounts and on-premises estates into roots with separate state
Give a team a repository boundary and a shared module, not a shared apply role
Promote a change from development to production by reviewing the same module at a new pin
Upgrade OpenTofu and providers as their own commits, with a plan attached

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Multi-Cloud and Hybrid Infrastructure: Managing AWS, Azure, GCP, and On-Premises Together
text:
Multi-Cloud and Hybrid Infrastructure: Managing AWS, Azure, GCP, and On-Premises Together
One root module may talk to several providers. A root that talks to all of them because they appear on one architecture slide is a root that fails when any one of them fails, and that only one team is allowed to apply.
Split by blast radius and by credential:








Root
Owns
Does not own




identity
The accounts, folders, and projects other roots use
The networks inside them


network
Shared networks, once per cloud account
Application buckets


app-<name>
That application’s resources in one account
The shared network. It takes ids as variables or remote outputs


onprem-<site>
Appliances and DNS at that site
The cloud account, except for a narrow handoff such as a VPN endpoint id



Hybrid is two roots and an explicit handoff value, not one configuration with every provider alias. The on-premises provider’s token and the cloud role should not sit in the same pipeline job unless the change truly crosses that line in one apply. Most changes do not.
Naming and tags carry the root’s identity into the console: managed-by=opentofu, the root name, and the repository URL. A human who edits the object can see who will overwrite the edit.

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Organizational Structure: Team-Based Repository Layouts and Shared Responsibility
text:
Organizational Structure: Team-Based Repository Layouts and Shared Responsibility
A layout that matches the way reviews work:
infra/
├── modules/                 # versioned when more than one root calls them
│   └── pets/
├── roots/
│   ├── pets-dev/
│   │   ├── versions.tf
│   │   ├── backend.tf
│   │   └── main.tf          # calls modules/pets
│   └── pets-prod/
└── policy/                  # Rego, pinned by the pipeline
The team that owns the application owns roots/pets-* and reviews those plans. A platform team owns modules/ and the policy repository. They do not need to approve every pet-name change. They do need to approve a new major of a module the application roots pin.
A monorepo is fine when one organisation wants one history. Many repositories are fine when ownership is the point. Do not split so far that a module and its only caller move in lockstep across a version boundary for no reason. Do not stay monolithic so far that a plan for a sandbox prints the production network.
CODEOWNERS, or the equivalent, maps directories to reviewers. The apply role for pets-prod is assumable by the production pipeline, not by every developer token. Developers plan in dev. They open a pull request for prod. Chapter 13 is that pipeline.

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Environment Strategy: Development, Staging, Production Separation Patterns
text:
Environment Strategy: Development, Staging, Production Separation Patterns
Separate roots, separate backend keys, separate roles. Development may use smaller instances and may allow destroy. Production sets prevent_destroy on the data you cannot recreate and requires the approval gate.
Promotion is “the prod root moves its module pin from 1.4.2 to 1.5.0”, not “we apply the dev workspace with a different variable.” The module version is the artifact. The root’s variables are the environment. If prod and dev call different code, you are not promoting. You are maintaining two systems.
Staging exists when a change can break a dependency you cannot see in dev, such as a provider behaviour against a real load balancer. It is another root, smaller than production, with production-like configuration. It is not a workspace name inside the production state.
Ephemeral environments, one per pull request, are a root created by automation with a backend key that includes the request id, destroyed when the request closes. They need a budget, a janitor for leftovers, and a ban on using production data. They are a later optimisation, not the first layout.

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Versioning and Upgrades: OpenTofu Versions, Provider Updates, and Breaking Changes
text:
Versioning and Upgrades: OpenTofu Versions, Provider Updates, and Breaking Changes
Keep a matrix and look at it on a schedule. As of 21 October 2026 the supported OpenTofu lines are 1.13 (until 1 August 2027) and 1.12 (until 1 February 2027). 1.11 and older are out of security support. This book uses 1.13.2. A production estate on 1.6 is not “stable.” It is unpatched.
Upgrade OpenTofu in its own change:

Read the series changelog, including the breaking notes. For 1.13 those include WinRM provisioner removal, base64gzip byte changes, macOS 13, and the end of 32-bit builds
Bump the pin in mise or .terraform-version and required_version
tofu init and tofu plan in a non-production root
Read the plan. An empty plan is the goal. A surprise replace is a stop
Apply non-production, then production, with the normal gate

Provider upgrades are a different change, even when you do them the same week. -upgrade rewrites the lock file. Commit that diff alone. Major provider versions get a changelog reading and a plan in dev before prod’s pin moves.
Modules follow semver. A root that uses ~> 1.4 will take 1.4.z on the next init without a commit if you also forgot the lock. Commit the lock. Take minors on purpose.
Do not upgrade OpenTofu, the AWS provider, and the network module in one pull request. A bad plan then has three causes.

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Debugging and Logging: Tracing Failures in Complex Deployments
text:
Debugging and Logging: Tracing Failures in Complex Deployments
tofu plan and the error it prints are the first tool. Provider errors include the API message. Read it before you turn on tracing.
TF_LOG=info is enough for “which resource, which retry.” TF_LOG=trace is enormous and includes values that may be sensitive. Use trace on a throwaway reproduction, write it to a file you delete, and do not paste it into a ticket without reading it.
TF_LOG_PROVIDER=debug on one provider keeps the core quiet. TF_LOG_PATH writes the log to a file instead of mixing it with the plan.
When a plan hangs, it is usually a lock, a provider waiting on a credential, or a data source waiting on an API. Check the lock before you kill the process. Killing an apply can leave the lock and can leave an object half-created. The next plan tells you which. Resume from a clean init rather than from a half-written local .terraform.
Crash logs (crash.log) go with the bug report to the provider or to OpenTofu, not into the repository. Reproduce on 1.13.2 and the provider version from the lock file, or the report is incomplete.

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Real-World Case Studies: Production Patterns from Leading Organizations
text:
Real-World Case Studies: Production Patterns from Leading Organizations
Three patterns cover most estates this book is willing to call production. They are patterns, not claims about a particular company’s internals.
The single-application team. One repository, two roots (dev and prod), one module for the application, GitHub Actions with OIDC, state in a locked and encrypted bucket the application role cannot reconfigure. Plans on pull requests. Apply on main after one approval. This is the pet example grown up, and it is enough for a product company that is not a cloud provider.
The platform team and many application roots. The platform team publishes modules and Rego. Application teams pin them. Each application has its own state and its own role. The platform team does not apply application changes. A weekly job reports roots whose OpenTofu pin is not 1.13.x. The report is a pull request, not a silent upgrade.
The hybrid estate. Cloud roots as above. An on-premises root per site, with the appliance provider pinned and the token injected per job. The only shared values are outputs: an IP, a BGP peer, a DNS zone id. A change that touches both sides is two pull requests with an order written on them, applied in that order, each with an empty follow-up plan.
What all three refuse: a single state for every environment, a shared admin key, an apply from a laptop as the normal path, and an upgrade with no plan attached.

title: Enterprise-Scale Patterns and Production Operations
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Split roots by credential and blast radius, including on-premises sites
Teams own roots. A platform team owns shared modules and policy
Dev, staging, and prod are separate states. Promotion moves a module pin
Upgrade OpenTofu and providers in separate commits, on a supported series
Log at info first. Trace is a reproduction tool, and it leaks values
A production pattern has a locked backend, a role per root, and a plan in the pipeline

title: Conclusion: Delivering on the Infrastructure-as-Code Promise
text:
Conclusion: Delivering on the Infrastructure-as-Code Promise
Infrastructure as code is delivered when a second person can apply the same change you would have applied, from the commit you reviewed, and get an empty plan the next time. The binary being OpenTofu matters for the license, the pin, and a few features Terraform does not have. It does not change that test.

title: Conclusion: Delivering on the Infrastructure-as-Code Promise
section: What you can do this quarter
text:
What you can do this quarter
Start from the pet module and grow one real root. In order:

Pin OpenTofu 1.13.2. Commit the lock file and .gitignore before the first real resource
Put state in a backend with a lock, versioning, server-side encryption, and the client-side encryption block once you have somewhere to keep the key
Split variables, outputs, and provider configuration so a review has somewhere to look
Add tofu fmt, tofu validate, and either Trivy or Checkov to the pull request. Add one Rego rule you actually care about
Plan on the pull request. Apply on the protected branch with a role the laptop does not have
Import existing objects one group at a time, and stop when the plan is empty

A team that does those six things is operating OpenTofu. Workspaces, a controller inside Kubernetes, and a module published to the registry can wait until a second environment or a second caller makes them the smaller design.

title: Conclusion: Delivering on the Infrastructure-as-Code Promise
section: What the promise does not include
text:
What the promise does not include
The configuration is not the whole system. Consoles, controllers, and people with admin roles write to the same APIs. The plan is how you notice. Ignoring drift, or setting ignore_changes = all, gives the promise back.
Sentinel, HCP Terraform, and Stacks are not waiting inside the tofu binary. Policy is OPA. The control plane is your pipeline. Composition is a root module that calls children.
OpenTofu 1.13 and Terraform 1.17 are different tools that share an ancestor. Pin one per state. Read the changelog when the pin moves. The 1.13 series is supported until 1 August 2027, and support is not a permanent condition.

title: Conclusion: Delivering on the Infrastructure-as-Code Promise
section: From first principles to production
text:
From first principles to production
You define the end state in HCL. Providers make it true. State remembers the ids. Modules give that definition a boundary other people can call. Tests and policy keep the boundary honest. The pipeline is the only routine way the state is allowed to change.
That is the whole arc. The next apply should be boring.
